topIssues.title: kona-node: accept base64-encoded custom L1 chain configs
topIssues.author: joshklop
topIssues.body:
## Problem

Custom-L1 deployments may inject the L1 genesis through `KONA_NODE_L1_CHAIN_CONFIG` as base64-encoded JSON. `kona-node` currently parses that environment value as a `PathBuf` and calls `File::open`, so sufficiently large configs fail at startup with:

```
Error: Failed to open l1 config file: File name too long (os error 36)
```

This was observed with a netchef-managed custom-L1 devnet. The encoded genesis was about 52 KB and never reached JSON parsing.

## Proposed behavior

Keep accepting a file path, but fall back to standard base64-encoded JSON when the configured value is not a readable file. Support both forms already documented for custom L1 configuration:

- a directly encoded L1 chain config
- a genesis document with the L1 chain config under `.config`

Add unit coverage for file and base64 inputs so custom-L1 deployments do not regress.

topIssues.title: [PCD] Default-`X` benchmarking
topIssues.author: 0xOneTony
topIssues.body: `X` (the offset between the chosen L1 anchor's timestamp and the committed L2 `genesis_time`) must be large enough that `genesis_time` is still in the future when `OPCM.deploy()` is mined; otherwise `op-node` will produce empty filler blocks at L2 block time to fill the gap. Measure end-to-end runtime of the off-chain portion of the pipeline (anchor selection through prestate generation) against a real prestate builder, repeated enough times to get a stable result. Propose a default `X`.

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: add proposer L1 query ports
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
## Summary

- Introduce crate-private `L1View` and `QueryTime` ports for proposer observations.
- Add production adapters backed by the existing Alloy provider and contracts.
- Make `Proposer` non-generic while preserving its public constructor and policy behavior.
- Add focused characterization tests for read boundaries, failure isolation, and time handling.

## Why

This is the first in a series of changes that create independently controllable boundaries around the proposer’s external dependencies. These boundaries will enable deterministic scenario tests for complex lifecycle, failure, timing, and concurrency behavior without requiring live L1 infrastructure or real proofs.

Part of https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22171

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: add proposer superroot and execution ports
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
## Summary

- Introduce crate-private `SuperRootSource`, `ProofEngine`, and `ActionExecutor` ports.
- Add production adapters backed by the existing superroot client, SP1 proof pipeline, signer, and contracts.
- Route proposal, defense, and transaction effects through these ports while preserving policy and error classification.
- Add focused characterization tests for superroot validation, proof execution, and transaction outcomes.

## Why

This is the second in a series of changes that create independently controllable boundaries around the proposer’s external dependencies. Building on #22476, these ports isolate superroot queries, proof execution, and transaction submission so deterministic scenario tests can control each failure domain without requiring live infrastructure or real proofs.

Part of https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22171

topPRs.title: kona-node: Serve the system config lookup from imported blocks
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
> Stacked on #22465.

The sequencer's attributes builder and the derivation pipeline each reconstruct the `SystemConfig` of the block they are building on top of, once per block. That block is one the node has just imported, yet both fetched it back from the execution layer **in full** — the sequencer on the block-production path.

The obvious fix, fetching a header plus the first transaction instead of a whole block, is not available: both clients read L2 blocks over the **authenticated Engine API port**, which exposes only a subset of the `eth_` namespace, and `eth_getTransactionByBlock{Number,Hash}AndIndex` is not in it. See [the constraint write-up](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22432#issuecomment-5297533301) — this is very likely why both clients fetch full blocks in the first place.

So this removes the fetch instead of shrinking it.

`InsertTask` already decodes every payload it inserts in order to derive the block's `L2BlockInfo`, and `SealTask` and `ConsolidateTask` both route through it, so every imported block passes one point holding exactly the `(OpBlock, L2BlockInfo)` pair that `kona-providers-local`'s `BufferedL2Provider` stores — and then drops it. A new `ImportedBlockSink` hands it over instead, and `BufferedAlloyL2ChainProvider` sits in front of the RPC provider so the lookup reads the buffer first.

`ConsolidateTask` feeds the buffer too. It already fetches that block in full to compare against the derived attributes, and the next attributes built are that block's child asking for its config — so the buffer is hit at distance ~1 regardless of how far the safe head trails the unsafe head.

Only the hash-keyed lookup is served locally. A height does not identify a block across a reorg, so the by-number lookups stay on the authoritative RPC, and an entry for a block that is later reorged out is never returned — it just ages out. That means no reorg-event plumbing and no canonicality bookkeeping.

The second commit takes `ChainStateBuffer` off `tokio::sync::RwLock`. No guard was ever held across an await point — the one place it could have been dropped its guard by hand first — so the async locks bought nothing while forcing `block_imported` to be async and `#[async_trait]` to box a future per imported block. On `std::sync::RwLock` the buffer, the provider's write API and the sink are all synchronous, `providers-local` no longer needs a tokio runtime dependency, and the compiler now enforces "never hold a lock across an await" instead of a convention doing it.

Not addressed here: sync-start walk-back, `FinalizeTask` and cold lookups still fetch whole blocks. Those need the EL-side follow-up in #22432.

Part of #22432.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5*

topPRs.title: rust: tag upstream mirrors and extend reth bump-review guidance
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
Several op-crates carry code that mirrors upstream reth, revm or alloy — ports, verbatim
copies, overridden defaults, and re-declared surfaces. Nothing marked them, so an upstream
change that should force a matching edit here produces no diff and no compile error, and the
divergence is only found by someone reading both sides.

**Tags.** Each site gets ``UPSTREAM-MIRROR(<kind>): <crate>@<version> `<symbol>` ``, recording the
version the mirror was last verified against. Kinds are `port`, `copy`, `override`, `set` and
`delegate`.

**Tooling.** `rust/scripts/upstream-mirrors.py` (`just mirrors`) lists every tag and flags any
whose recorded version has fallen behind the pin; `--check` fails on a malformed tag. Current
state: **24 mirrors, 20 current, 4 frozen.**

**Guides.** `docs/ai/reth-upstream-mirrors.md` covers the grammar, the kinds, and which repo to
diff a `reth` mirror against. `docs/ai/reth-update-review.md` and `rust/UPDATING-RETH.md` gain
matching bump-review guidance, including triaging the fork's cherry-picks on each bump: list
what the branch carries on top of its upstream base, drop what has landed upstream, replay what
has not, and ask when an upstream equivalent was squashed or rewritten.

No behaviour changes — comments, docs and one new script.

### Follow-up

The tags describe the duplication; they do not reduce it. #22478 tracks the reduction work:
delegating where a seam already exists, deleting outright duplicates, and asking upstream for
abstractions where none exists today.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5*
